newsitem.title: GERMANY: German industry output rebounds in November.
newsitem.headline: German industry output rebounds in November.

text.p: German industrial production broke a two-month downturn to grow strongly in November, putting the economy back on course to hit modest 1996 growth targets ahead of an expected slack first quarter, analysts said on Friday.

Industrial output rose in November by 1.6 percent against October, seasonally adjusted data released by the Economics Ministry on Friday showed. October's output fall was revised down by over half to 0.7 percent.
Compared with the previous year, November output was up 1.3 percent after a 0.9 percent gain in October, the preliminary data showed.
The gain exceeded market expectations and eased fears among economists that Germany would miss a modest overall target of 1.5 percent growth in gross domestic product (GDP) for 1996.
"The production rise was to be expected given the rise in orders in October. It doesn't change our forecast that German GDP rose 1.5 percent in 1996," said Uwe Angenendt at BHF-Bank.
On a quarterly basis, economists said they expected fourth quarter GDP to be stagnant or slightly higher after strong second and third quarter growth.

But with snow blanketing Germany, pension contributions climbing to record levels from the start of the year, and tax breaks being scrapped, the first quarter is also likely to be flat, Angenendt told Reuters.
Rob Hayward at Bank of America in London said that the cold weather threatened a repeat of last winter's weather-related economic setback -- and could even be worse this year.

"Growth in the fourth quarter will be flat at best and there may even be a small contraction. If we are looking at any growth in the consumer side we can forget about it. The economy will remain weak," Hayward told Reuters Financial Television.
The industrial output data for November showed broad gains in manufacturing, with consumer durables leading with a gain of 4.2 percent. Construction activity was down by two percent.

German industrial production data are notoriously volatile and often subject to heavy revisions, and a broader comparison of the latest two months against August and September showed output unchanged overall.
Separate trade data published for October confirmed the picture that Germany's recovery is being led by exports.

October exports were up 14 percent on a year earlier to 74.9 billion marks ($48.25 billion), with the 10-month cumulative total up 4.7 percent to 648 billion marks. The October trade surplus widened to 11.1 billion marks from 8.3 billion.

With consumer demand weak and the economy still largely being carried by export growth, the overall picture was still subdued and left some scope for the Bundesbank to ease its repo interest rate, currently at three percent, analysts said.

"We have low M3 (money supply), high unemployment, low productivity and a reduced picture for GDP so I think the Bundesbank will come under pressure to act on the repo side," said Michael Hochgurtel, also at BHF Bank.

Although the economy is expected to grow by over two percent this year, that will not be enough to tackle Germany's jobs crisis, and Hayward predicted that unemployment would soar to 4.5 million by February.
December unemployment data are due for publication next Thursday after the seasonally-adjusted November jobless total climbed to 4.1 million. ($1=1.5492 Mark)
